newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Political rows brews ahead of Yeltsin operation.
newsitem.headline: Political rows brews ahead of Yeltsin operation.

text.p: Russia began the countdown for President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation on Wednesday in an atmosphere soured by a row among top Moscow politicians and new tensions between the Kremlin and powerful regional bosses.

Kremlin spokesman Igor Ignatyev said preparations for the operation were going according to plan and added that Yeltsin's doctors were waiting for pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey's to join them on Monday to decide the date for surgery.
DeBakey, quoted by the British Broadcasting Corporation, said the operation could take place next week.
"We're shooting for next week, but I can't be any more specific than that because we'll probably be meeting on Monday with the medical team and making that decision," he said.
DeBakey said doctors were expecting three or four bypasses. The Russian operating team will be led by cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who will use equipment from DeBakey's Houston centre.

But as Yeltsin awaited his doctors' decision at a sanatorium near Moscow, the head of the lower house of parliament demanded the sacking of the president's chief-of-staff, upsetting plans to make different state organs work more closely together.

The State Duma chairman Gennady Seleznyov said he was not happy with the appointment of controversial businessman Boris Berezovsky as deputy secretary of Yeltsin's Security Council -- an advisory board comprising top officials.

Communist Seleznyov accused the chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais of engineering Berzovsky's nomination and said he would not take part in a newly established consultative council on which Chubais is also due to sit.

Yeltsin, 65, had hoped the four-member council, which also includes Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Yegor Stroyev, head of the upper chamber of parliament, would help avert the in-fighting that has plagued recent Russian politics.

"I insist on the immediate dismissal of the president's head of administration Anatoly Chubais. I do not doubt that I am expressing the opinion of an absolute majority of Russian citizens," said a Seleznyov statement distributed in the Duma.
Chubais, brought into the Kremlin in July, has long been a hate figure for Russia's communists, who despise his privatisation programme and the free-market economic reforms he helped to launch.

The communist-dominated Duma has already locked horns with the government over the 1997 budget, which deputies say includes unrealistic spending plans and provides too little to support the poor, including those who have not been paid for months.
A commission of parliamentarians and ministers aimed at finding a compromise budget held its first meeting on Wednesday.
Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said he expected salary arrears to be cleared this year and Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin said he expected the economy to start to grow in 1997.
Yeltsin has already handed some powers over to Chernomyrdin and the premier will take charge during the surgery, which will relieve clogged arteries supplying blood to Yeltsin's heart.

In another upset to Yeltsin's team some influential regional leaders made clear they were not happy with the latest Moscow's crusade aimed at consolidating the Kremlin's control over 89 regions and ethnic republics which form the Russian Federation.

Chubais blamed the regional leadership for encouraging legislation which violated nationoal constitution. He said the Kremlin would take tough measures to ensure that nothing is done in Russia which would violate Moscow's interests.

Interfax news agency quoted the head of the ethnic republic of North Ossetia, Akhsarbek Galazov, as warning the Kremlin that "any attack on regional powers amounts to damaging the powers of Russia as a whole."
"Any humiliation of regional power will help Russia's enemies," added Galazov, generally known for his pro-Moscow views. "Then a threat of separatism could emerge."
